  - list:
    - listitem: Predict how each solid will change. Keep the ice and salt in separate vessels.
    - listitem: Record the initial masses and temperatures. The ice begins at 0 °C; the salt vessel stays at 25 °C.
    - listitem: Pause during melting and just before and after its predicted completion. Record ice, melted water, sample temperature and heat.
    - listitem: At the same time, record solid salt, dissolved salt and solution mass. Check each vessel’s mass budget separately.
    - listitem: Compare fresh no-heat, still-water and little-solvent controls, changing one setting at a time and matching elapsed time.
    - listitem: Use the worked substitutions. State a result, explain phase change versus solution formation, and write a limitation.
  - text: Prediction
  - textbox "Comparison prediction": Ice needs heat to change into liquid water. Salt can dissolve in separate water without becoming molten salt. Stirring should change the chosen rate, while less solvent can leave excess salt. Both vessels should conserve their own matter.

  - generic "Worked heat, melting, dissolving and concentration substitutions"
  - text: Result, conclusion and limitation
  - textbox "Comparison conclusion"
  - paragraph: Advanced calculations are a teacher extension. Initially ice is at its melting point. Bath and solution temperatures are maintained; conductance and dissolution rates are chosen. No vessel heat capacity, evaporation, solution enthalpy or resolved heat/fluid flow is solved. Ice is a uniformly shrinking reference cube; 60 salt grains encode solid mass rather than measured morphology. Left geometry accounts for water and displaced ice; the right fill is schematic because solution volume is not solved. Stirrer motion illustrates a condition, not a computed vortex. The latest 60 observations remain in this browser.
